executive_summary: GBP/JPY closed at 209.01289 on 2026-10-02 in the gated price store. That close is one session after the 2026-10-01 valuation date, and every level in this report is anchored to it. The pair is quoted in yen per pound, so a rising GBP/JPY means sterling is strengthening against the yen. The pair is down 0.81% over one month, 3.49% over three months and 2.17% over six months, and up 3.18% over one year. It sits at the 46th percentile of its 52-week closing range (199.95-219.61), below its 50-, 100- and 200-day simple averages (212.64 / 214.00 / 213.10) and 8.4% above a rising 200-week average at 192.88. The pair is caught between carry and convergence. A 250bp policy gap (Bank Rate 3.75% against the BoJ's 1.25%) pays a rolled long about 2.76% a year on the CME 6B/6J calendar spread. But the BoJ has guided that it will keep hiking, and the UK curve already prices almost all of one BoE hike. The bilateral signal is much stronger than either dossier alone, and three things explain why: the sterling dossier's only bullish factor (rates) explicitly excludes the yen and lists the GBP-JPY gap as narrowing to 225bp; the yen dossier's bearish factors are mostly about the dollar; and there is a direct gilt channel, since Japanese real money has already sold gilts heavily when UK fiscal fears rose. The settled verdict is tactically Neutral at conviction 1 (score -0.0508). The sterling-specific Budget and fiscal risk on 28 October is offset by crowded positioning against the pair: sterling short and yen long, both facing unwind triggers three sessions apart, and both central-bank decisions fall just after the four-week window. The verdict is strategically Bearish at conviction 3 (score -0.4024). Our base case is 202.00 by end-Q1 2027, a 3.36% fall and 413 pips below the derived six-month forward of 206.13. The main caveat is carry. A short paid on spot costs about 288 pips over six months, and seven of the bearish factors share one policy-convergence mechanism. We therefore recommend entering after 5 November by selling the four-touch resistance band at 210.66-211.95, with a stop above 214.10. Published consensus disagrees: the Exchange Rates UK aggregate projects the Pound-Yen exchange rate at 212.99 in one month and 209.90 in six months.

market_context.recent_regime: GBP/JPY topped at 219.65 in mid-July, then fell in steps. The dominant narrative has shifted from carry to convergence, but the market is waiting for the late-October cluster before committing.

bilateral_carry_analysis.carry_assessment: Policy carry is +250bp to a long (BoE 3.75% minus BoJ 1.25%), and the actual roll economics are better: the CME 6B/6J calendar-spread funding premium is -276.3bp annualised (observed 2026-09-30), so a rolled long earns about 2.76% a year. The 26bp over the policy gap is basis plus expected policy path, which cannot be separated without an OIS curve. In pips that is about 522 a year (43.5 a month) at 250bp or about 577 a year (48 a month) at 276bp, at spot 209.01. Carry-to-vol is 0.32 on the 7.927% estimated 3-month implied using the 250bp policy carry (0.35 on the 276.3bp roll; 0.30 on 60-day realised of 8.22%), and because the implied estimate runs low the ratio is an upper bound. The carry is large but not protective, since rate convergence means it is earned and then given back in spot. A short carries this cost explicitly, so a strategic bearish view must beat the forward, not spot, to be paid.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Bank Rate at 3.75% against a BoJ call-rate target of 1.25% gives a 250bp policy differential in sterling's favour (payload policyDifferential 2.50). The payload's 10-year gap of 205bp is a monthly vintage from 2026-08-01 and is not used as a live level; on the dossiers' 30 September prints (gilt 5.42%, JGB 3.05-3.07%) the gap is about 236bp. The carry is real and is what a rolled position actually earns: the CME 6B/6J calendar-spread funding premium is -276.3bp annualised, so a long GBP/JPY futures roll collects roughly 2.76% a year, about 26bp above the policy gap (basis plus expected path, which cannot be separated without an OIS curve). The pricing asymmetry runs against that carry. The UK curve carries almost 80% of a 5 November hike and about 39bp to December, close to the ceiling, and the GBP dossier puts the hike at 70%. The Japanese curve carries only about 25-38% for 30 October and about 39% by 18 December, while the BoJ says it 'will continue raising' rates, and the JPY dossier puts October at 40-45%. Neither decision falls inside the four-week window, which ends 29 October; the BoJ meets a day after it. So over the tactical horizon the differential reprices only in anticipation and through the 21 October UK CPI. A wide positive carry level is offset by surprise risk on both legs, each of which would narrow the differential relative to pricing. That is Neutral.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: On a one-to-three month view, what matters is the first derivative of the differential, not its level, and the two dossiers' base cases together point to compression. The GBP dossier's central path is one BoE hike to 4.00% on 5 November (Monetary Policy Report) and then a stop, capped by AWE regular pay slowing to 3.5% and settlements to 3.6%. The JPY dossier's central path is two further BoJ hikes to 1.75%, with three decision dates in the gated calendar inside the window: 30 October (Outlook Report), 18 December and 22 January 2027 (Outlook Report). That takes the gap from 250bp to about 225bp, while the curve prices it modestly wider by December. The GBP dossier's own strategic Bullish rates call rests explicitly on CHF, SEK and CAD, where differentials widen; it lists GBP-JPY as narrowing to +225bp. On the long end, the JGB 10y has risen 141bp in a year and now trades above Bunds. The gilt's extra yield is increasingly a fiscal term premium rather than a growth premium, so it is a weaker currency support than its size implies. The level of carry stays large and positive, which is why confidence is held at 55 and not higher. The direction of travel, and the surprise against pricing, both favour the yen.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: UK inflation runs well above Japan's on every measure: August UK headline 3.1%, core 2.6% and services 3.4%, against Japanese headline 1.9%, core ex fresh food 1.7% and core-core 1.9%. That is about 120bp on headline and 70-90bp on the core measures. The JPY dossier's GBP row carries stale vintages (headline 2.9%, core 3.2%); the GBP dossier's August ONS prints are used instead. Underneath the gap, both economies are importing an energy shock rather than generating domestic demand pressure. UK core and services were flat while motor fuels drove the headline. Japanese core is suppressed by electricity subsidies (electricity -2.4% y/y) sitting under a 7.6% producer price index. Growth slightly favours the UK: Q2 GDP +0.5% q/q and 1.4% y/y against Japan's +0.36% q/q and 0.73% y/y, with UK PMIs at 51.7. Japan's consumption contributed zero to Q2 GDP and the October Tankan missed at +24. The data dates inside the window are two-sided: Japanese wages on 6 October and household spending on 8 October, then UK CPI on 21 October, the last print before the Budget and the MPC. Neither economy is clearly outrunning the other on the data that moves its central bank. Neutral.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months both economies face a stagflationary energy impulse, and the two dossiers read it differently for their own currencies. In the UK, the BoE projects CPI 'slightly over 4% in early 2027', driven by a January Ofgem cap forecast 16% higher at GBP1,999. Against real regular pay growth of +0.6%, that pushes real household income negative in Q1 2027; the GBP dossier calls this a currency negative through growth even though it is rate-supportive. In Japan, the subsidy-suppressed core sits under a 7.6% PPI, the 2026 Shunto settled at 5.01% and Tankan three-year inflation expectations are 2.6%. Inflation risk is therefore skewed up, which would give the BoJ cover to keep hiking. But real wages are negative for a fourth year, household spending is -3.6% y/y and potential growth is only 0.5-1%. Bilaterally, UK inflation rising is mostly imported and growth-destructive, while Japanese inflation rising is the mechanism that would carry the BoJ further. That leans against the pair, but the inflation level gap itself still supports BoE rates staying high. These offset, and the relative policy consequence is already scored in Factor 1. Neutral, with no double count.

The VIX is 16.07 (+1.64 on the month), US investment grade is unchanged at 83bp, and US high yield is 42bp wider at 302bp, the early signature of risk appetite fraying at the low-quality end. With the VIX expected to hold 14-20, the haven channel stays dormant over four weeks. If it activates, though, it works against the pair on both legs, through yen repatriation and carry unwind and through sterling's gilt-linked crisis correlation. Without a trigger in the window, the asymmetry belongs in the strategic stance. Neutral.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the risk factor is an asymmetry argument, and for this cross the asymmetry points one way. Starting from IG at 83bp and the VIX at 16, the distribution of changes is skewed toward widening. The yen is the G10's highest-beta beneficiary of a widening, through repatriation of roughly USD3.5tn of Japanese foreign securities and through carry unwind. Sterling is among the most exposed losers, because the UK carries the largest term premium in the G10 and 25-30% foreign gilt ownership, and the GBP dossier's crisis correlation has gilts and sterling falling together. A continued melt-up helps the pair less than a risk-off hurts it, since GBP/JPY carry is already overwhelmed by rate convergence. The offset is that the yen's carry-unwind fuel is largely spent (JPY speculative positioning swung from -92.2K to +72.0K), which reduces the magnitude but not the sign. An Iran re-escalation is two-sided for Japan (haven bid against an energy shock) but also hits UK gas. Bearish at low confidence; a risk shock is not the base case.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Positioning extremes discharge around events. Beyond late October the flow that matters for this cross is institutional, and its direct bilateral channel is Japanese demand for gilts. Long-dated JGBs now out-yield currency-hedged foreign bonds at 3-4% hedge costs; the JGB 10y crossed 3% on 1 September 2026 for the first time since 1996, which TD Securities called a regime change. The bilateral record shows the channel is live and fiscally sensitive. Japanese investors bought a net ¥418.6bn of UK debt in October 2025, then made the largest net sales since 2011, ¥351.4bn, in November 2025, citing UK fiscal concerns and higher domestic yields. The UK relies on overseas holders for 25-30% of gilts, and the DMO is cutting long issuance because domestic DB demand is shrinking, so any Japanese retreat from duration falls on the marginal buyer. Japan's fiscal year-end (2027-03-31) adds a seasonal repatriation impulse at the edge of the strategic window. The offset is that weekly Japanese foreign-bond buying was still +¥1,082.9bn in mid-September, so the repatriation trend is noisy. Bearish at moderate confidence.

tactical.contrarian_case: The case against the crowd is that both the bad Budget and the hawkish BoJ are well telegraphed, and a well-telegraphed risk delivered on schedule is usually worth less than the premium paid for it. If the Chancellor produces a rule-compliant Budget and the BoJ waits until December, the cross faces simultaneous short covering in sterling and long liquidation in yen. That is why Factor 4 is the main tactical offset to Factors 7 and 8.

strategic.combined_positioning_signal: Neutralising: after the 28 Oct to 5 Nov cluster both IMM extremes are expected to normalise (the JPY dossier says four to eight weeks after an extreme), leaving institutional duration flows as the operative signal.
strategic.unwind_trigger: Not applicable in the speculative sense; the strategic risk is the reverse, a rebuild of yen-funded carry if the BoJ stalls at 1.25% and US/UK yields rise again.
strategic.historical_analogue: Japanese gilt flows in Oct-Nov 2025: record purchases followed one month later by the largest sales since 2011 on UK fiscal concern, showing Japanese gilt demand is highly fiscally sensitive.
strategic.contrarian_case: The contrarian risk to a strategic Bearish view is that yen carry has rebuilt on this configuration many times before. With the VIX at 16 and a 250bp differential, a BoJ that pauses would make GBP/JPY a funding-currency long again. A credible Budget could also re-attract Japanese real money to 5%-plus gilts, as happened in October 2025.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Both legs are net energy importers, so the bilateral question is which is hit harder by which fuel. Recent prints cut both ways. The UK Q2 current account beat expectations at -2.5% of GDP (-GBP19.9bn against -GBP25.6bn expected) as the trade deficit halved. Japan's August goods balance was -¥1,105.6bn, the fourth consecutive deficit, with crude imports up 58.7%; its 5.03%-of-GDP current account surplus rests on primary income that is largely reinvested abroad rather than converted into yen. On commodities, Brent has fallen to about USD97-98 from the cache's stale USD114.89. Under the framework's direction rules, falling oil is a larger relief for the yen (--JPY sensitivity) than for sterling (-GBP), a mild pair negative. UK NBP gas has not followed crude (182.89p, +128.6% y/y), which weighs on sterling. The direct trade link is small and balanced: IMF DOTS shows UK goods exports to Japan of USD9.3bn against imports of USD8.6bn (2024), a +USD0.7bn UK surplus. Japan's mirror records exports to the UK of USD11.2bn against imports of USD7.9bn; the asymmetry is recorded, not resolved. Either way the bilateral flow is too small to drive the pair. The window contains Japan's current account on 7 October and no UK external print. Neutral.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: At a 0.16 weight this is the second-heaviest strategic factor, and the structural external gap favours the yen. The UK runs a persistent current account deficit (-2.5% of GDP headline) whose primary income line has swung to a GBP3.8bn quarterly deficit, as payments to foreign holders of UK assets outgrow receipts at 1999-high gilt yields. Japan holds the world's largest net international investment position (about USD3.3tn), with a ¥4.29tn July primary income surplus that puts a floor under its current account. The valuation gap is extreme and points the same way. On the BIS broad real basis sterling is 112.33, third richest in the set, and the yen 66.02, the cheapest by 28.8 points. The GBP dossier's REER-relative proxy puts sterling about 70% rich to the yen, and the JPY dossier's estimate puts the yen about 26% cheap. That is a constraint on the upside rather than a timing signal, and confidence reflects it. The offset is Japan's energy dependence. Under the direction rules, oil and LNG rises hit the yen harder than sterling, and Japan sources 94.2% of its crude from the Middle East. So the bearish stance is conditional on Brent staying near current levels rather than re-spiking. Bearish at moderate confidence.

net_commodity_exposure.base_commodity_profile: GBP: net energy importer with declining North Sea output and limited gas storage. Key terms-of-trade input is UK NBP / European gas (TTF up means -GBP), with oil a secondary negative (oil up means -GBP).
net_commodity_exposure.quote_commodity_profile: JPY: imports about 99% of its oil, 94.2% of crude from the Middle East, and is a large LNG importer. Oil up means --JPY; LNG (JKM) up means --JPY.
net_commodity_exposure.net_effect_calculation: Oil: GBP (-) vs JPY (--), so the yen is hit harder and oil up is net pair-POSITIVE (GBP/JPY rises); oil down is net pair-negative. LNG/JKM: only the JPY rule applies (--JPY), so LNG up is pair-positive. TTF/NBP gas: only the GBP rule applies (-GBP), so European gas up is pair-NEGATIVE. Netting: a broad energy rally (oil and LNG with gas) is mildly pair-positive because the yen carries the double-negative on two fuels against sterling's single negative on two. A gas-specific European squeeze with crude falling, the current configuration of Brent down from about USD115 to about USD97 with NBP up 128.6% y/y, is pair-negative on both counts.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_up_10pct: Net pair-POSITIVE: Japan's goods deficit (already -¥1.1tn monthly) widens faster than the UK's oil bill, and the JPY dossier's 115-dollar invalidator moves closer. Partly offset if gas rises alongside, which hits sterling.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_down_10pct: Net pair-NEGATIVE: the larger relief accrues to Japan's crude-dependent import bill. If NBP gas stays elevated, sterling gets little offsetting relief.
net_commodity_exposure.dominant_commodity_driver: Brent crude for the pair (it carries the asymmetric JPY double-negative), with UK NBP gas as the sterling-specific secondary driver through the January Ofgem cap.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The two central banks are at opposite ends of the guidance cycle. The BoE has already converted its hawkish guidance into price: the 6-3 vote, the 'tilted to the upside' risk language and Lombardelli's 'increasingly likely to need to tighten' moved the curve to almost 80% for November. The GBP dossier notes guidance has no further hawkish room without delivery, and the Committee is speaking with two voices (Taylor sounding dovish the same week). The BoJ's guidance is ahead of its price. The September statement says the Bank 'will continue raising' rates, and the 30 September Summary of Opinions showed a majority favouring further hikes and one member arguing to accelerate, against a curve at 25-38% for October. Sequencing favours the yen: the BoJ's Outlook Report on 30 October comes six days before the BoE's MPR. Two things keep confidence low. Neither meeting falls inside the four-week window. And the Takaichi administration (parliamentary address 5 October) leans toward accommodation and is pressing the Bank to weigh past hikes, although the September hike was delivered under it. Bearish, modestly.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the cadence of scheduled forecast rounds favours the yen. The BoJ has two Outlook Reports in the window (2026-10-30, 2027-01-22) plus a decision on 2026-12-18. Each is a scheduled opportunity to raise the CPI path, and the JPY dossier argues the distribution around them is fat-tailed toward hawkish outcomes given a 5.01% Shunto, 2.6% Tankan expectations and a subsidy-suppressed core. The BoE has the 5 November MPR and a 17 December decision. The GBP dossier identifies the MPR as the most likely source of a dovish sterling shock: because the BoE conditions its forecast on market rates, a projection showing inflation back at target on a 39bp-hike curve would tell the market its pricing is too hawkish. The BoE also under-forecast August CPI by 30bp and has a 6-3 Committee whose median is hard to observe, so its guidance informs without anchoring. On the yen side, the joint US-Japan intervention commitment (Katayama and Bessent) is a new form of exchange-rate guidance that truncates the yen-weak tail across all crosses. The offset is the political constraint on the BoJ, which is real but already evidenced against.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Event risk inside the window is lopsided against sterling. The 28 October Budget and OBR Economic and Fiscal Outlook confront March headroom of GBP23.6bn that UBS estimates has already been eroded by about GBP24bn. It is the first Budget of a Burnham-Healey administration whose 'flexibility' signal moved the 30y gilt 9bp in a day, and ING judges that sterling carries no fiscal risk premium. The FOMC meets the same day, compounding the session. The yen leg's event risk is milder and two-sided. The 5 October Takaichi address is a modest yen negative on fiscal expansion. Against that, the late-July joint US-Japan intervention, which both governments say they would repeat, truncates the yen-weak tail on every yen cross. A Hormuz re-escalation is a haven bid for the yen but an energy shock for both; it hits UK gas directly. Options corroborate the UK side: 67% of Budget-week GBP/USD expiries are bearish on sterling against a 55% baseline. The positioning crowd (Factor 4) is the reason confidence is 62 rather than higher.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Once 28 October has passed, the residual event risk is more balanced, but it still leans against the pair. On the UK side, the DMO remit revision lands with the Budget, Ofgem announces the January cap in late November (forecast +16%, a political as well as economic event), and the post-Brexit slower-clock risks persist. No UK election is due. On the Japanese side, the December FY2027 budget compilation runs under explicit Fitch scrutiny, the JPY dossier puts snap-election risk at about 15%, and an expansionary Takaichi programme is a yen negative. Against those, the JPY dossier puts a second coordinated intervention at about 20% (conditional on USD/JPY revisiting 162) and a Hormuz re-escalation at about 15%. Both are yen-positive through the haven channel and the latter is also UK-gas negative. China-Taiwan is a low-probability, unambiguously yen-positive tail. Netting the two catalogues, the yen's dated political risk (the December budget) is roughly matched by sterling's (the remit and the Ofgem cap), while the geopolitical tails skew yen-positive. Bearish at low confidence.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: On headline metrics Japan is the weaker sovereign: debt is about 260% of GDP against the UK's 93.8%, and ratings are A1/A+/A against AA/Aa3. Over four weeks, though, only the UK side has a dated trigger and visible market stress. UK August borrowing overshot the OBR by GBP3.5bn (GBP8.1bn year to date), August debt interest was a record GBP8.8bn including GBP2.1bn of RPI uplift, the 30y gilt is at 5.96% and the 29 September 10y auction cleared at 5.383%, the highest since 1999. All of that lands into the 28 October Budget. Japan's fiscal tape is calm by comparison. The late-September 40y auction drew the strongest demand since 2020, the 2y cleared without incident, and JGB yields fell 2.5-4bp across the curve on 30 September on a fiscal-reassurance report. Funding structure matters more for the currency than the debt ratio: about 90% of JGBs are held domestically and the BoJ holds about half, while 25-30% of gilts are held overseas and the UK runs a current account deficit. A UK fiscal shock therefore transmits to sterling through the portfolio channel in a way Japan's does not transmit to the yen. Bearish.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months both sovereigns have chronic and worsening fiscal dynamics, and the bilateral net is close to zero. The UK's chain runs from imported energy to RPI-linked debt interest to a higher term premium and a wider primary income deficit, aggravated by DMO cuts to long issuance as domestic DB demand shrinks and by GBP20bn a year of QT sales. Debt/GDP is falling 1.3pp year on year, though, and no rating review is scheduled. Japan's fiscal-monetary circularity is tightening on a dated schedule. The JGB 30y at 4.15% against a 2y at 1.93% increasingly reflects term premium. Each 100bp on the average yield eventually costs about 2% of GDP. The December FY2027 budget under an expansionary administration faces Fitch scrutiny, and the JPY dossier puts a negative outlook at about 15%. Japan's risk is larger in stock; the UK's is more externally financed and therefore more currency-transmissive. These offset. A rise in JGB yields driven by term premium could even invert the yen's usual positive yield transmission, which would be pair-positive and cuts against the bearish factors elsewhere. Neutral.

That improves the Japanese domestic alternative to foreign duration in general, but its pair-specific effect runs through gilts (Factor 4), not through the dollar as such. December year-end dollar funding demand reliably widens the yen basis seasonally, a modest yen negative, while the GBP basis is normally tight. On the dollar smile, both currencies underperform on the risk-off left side (sterling by fiscal exposure, the yen by funding role historically, though less so now). The net for the cross is negligible. Neutral.

tactical.rationale: At tactical weights the pair is decided by Policy & Rates (0.24), Inflation & Growth (0.18) and Risk Appetite (0.12), which carry 54% of the weight, and all three are Neutral. For rates that is the correct reading, not an evasion. signposts.invalidates_if: It widens beyond -300bp, meaning carry is being repriced wider

signposts.invalidates_if: It falls below 5.60% for five sessions
signposts.bilateral_importance: It triggers sterling's crisis correlation and drives Japanese duration allocation away from gilts, so it matters more for GBP/JPY than for EUR/GBP, where Bunds move with it.

assumptions: Spot timing: spotDate (2026-10-02) is one session after the 2026-10-01 valuation date. Every level, pip distance, percentage, forward outright and scenario target is anchored to 209.01289. No web quote is substituted.

Price payload metadata: dataPoints 130; dateRange 2026-04-06 to 2026-10-02; computationRange 2007-12-24 to 2026-10-02 (4900 weekday bars); dataQuality: GBP/JPY 4900 weekday bars in the store, 1007 weekly, 500 monthly; 130 daily bars passed downstream, which is the 1-6 month strategic horizon.

Moving averages are simple averages of trading-day closes computed over the whole stored history. The 200-week (192.87922, slope +0.262397 a week, zero weeks since the last close above it) is treated as a first-class structural level; its projection to about 199.6 by end-March 2027 is linear arithmetic from the payload slope.

Zones are taken from the payload's clustered weekly and monthly swing closes, ranked by touch count; distances are quoted to the zone midpoint. Daily swing lows (206.89, 207.09, 207.28) are read from OHLC bars and labelled as non-zone levels.

Realised vol (6.91% over 20 days, 8.22% over 60) is from the payload. Implied vol is the store's triangle ESTIMATE (pair_3m_iv 7.927% at 99.7 days), treated as a floor because the method has run 8.7-17.8% low against direct quotes. There is no quoted cross risk reversal; skew is inferred from the legs and labelled as inference.
The funding premium (-276.3bp, 6B/6J, observed 2026-09-30) is interest differential plus basis, not a policy differential. Forward outrights are derived from it on a linear day-count, not quoted.

Direction verdict: factors and synthesis (stances, confidences, evidence types, weights, contributions, net scores, convictions, rationales, rankings, consensus and cross-horizon text) are carried verbatim from pass 1, which scored without the price payload. Pass 2 added market context, carry, scenarios, path, conviction ladders, risk/reward, forwards, invalidators, signposts and price-level expression. The Factor 9 price-structure addendum is outside the score. One tactical reservation on the composition of the sterling short is published in the consensus section without re-scoring.

Policy rates come from the event store (BoE 3.75%, BoJ 1.25%). The payload's 10-year yields are monthly vintages from 2026-08-01 and are not quoted as live. Dossier conflicts are resolved toward the more recent or verified figure, including Fed QT having ended on 2025-12-01. BoJ OIS probabilities are used directionally only. IMF DOTS mirror asymmetries are recorded, not resolved.

Scenario probabilities follow the framework's 50/25/25 convention and are subjective. Strategic targets are anchored to computed zones (202.00 in the 201.94-203.45 band; 196.50 in 195.77-197.65; 214.00 at the 100-day and top of the 212.80-213.89 band) and cross-checked against the product of the two dossiers' base cases (about 194), judged too aggressive given the secular uptrend and the four-touch floor.

Web research was limited to pair-specific forecasts, chart-pattern commentary, gilt-flow evidence and carry commentary. No spot, performance, moving-average, volatility or support/resistance figure was taken from the web. Extrapolation-script forecast sites (LongForecast, 30rates, CoinCodex, Traders Union and similar) were excluded as category errors; community chart ideas carry low provenance and are used for pattern identification only.

Formatter notes: the source does not state CFTC percentile ranks or an IV percentile, so base_cftc_percentile, quote_cftc_percentile and iv_percentile are null rather than invented. Dossier dates are not stated in the source and are set to the valuation date.

Formatter notes: annualised_carry_bps uses the 276.3bp funding roll (positive = a long earns), so carry_to_vol_ratio is computed as 2.763/7.927 = 0.35; the report's 0.32 uses the 250bp policy carry. Factor 1's carry_analysis retains the report's 0.32.

Formatter notes: the report gives week-level timing for the Ofgem cap (2026-11-W4) and the Japan FY2027 budget compilation (2026-12-W3); schema-required dates 2026-11-27 and 2026-12-15 are approximations. The aggregator consensus is quoted differently in the report (212.99 / 209.90 in the executive summary and pass-2 table; 212.43 / 209.92 in the consensus section); both are retained.
